disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c of 6.5 falls in the diabetes range, and your body weight is above the healthy range, which together with your age can raise your overall health risks. The good news is that regular activity, following a calorie target of about 1700 calories a day, and keeping up with monitoring like vitamin B12 checks and a cardiovascular risk assessment can make a real difference. Prioritizing fasting and post-meal blood sugar checks along with a lipid profile will help you and your doctor track changes over time. These steps, taken together, can help support steadier blood sugar and better overall wellness.

foods_to_eat: Leafy greens like bok choy and spinach
Whole grains such as brown rice, millet and buckwheat
Tofu, tempeh and edamame for plant protein
Seaweed and mushrooms for fibre and minerals
Unsweetened soy milk and soy yogurt
Nuts and seeds like sesame and walnuts
Non-starchy vegetables such as cabbage, carrots and bell peppers
foods_to_avoid: Sugary drinks like bubble tea and soda
White rice in large portions and refined noodles
Deep-fried items such as tempura and spring rolls
Processed snacks high in salt and sugar
Pastries and cakes made with refined flour
plan.portion_guidance: Fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with whole grains like millet or brown rice, and one quarter with a plant protein such as tofu or tempeh. Keep rice or noodle portions to about half to one cup per meal to support steady blood sugar.
plan.hydration: Aim for 8 to 10 glasses of water through the day. Unsweetened green tea is a good addition, but avoid sweetened bubble teas and bottled drinks.
based_on: HbA1c in the diabetes range: low-glycaemic, high-fibre focus

exercise: Since you're already moderately active, build toward at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity like brisk walking, cycling, or swimming, spread across most days.
Add muscle-strengthening activities (like bodyweight exercises, resistance bands, or light weights) on 2 non-consecutive days a week.
Increase intensity or duration gradually, by about 10% every week or two, rather than jumping up quickly.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Start with 20-25 minutes of brisk walking most days this week, then build up to at least 30 minutes on 5 or more days a week over the next month.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI falls in the overweight category, so gently working toward a modest reduction in body weight can help support your HbA1c goals. Focus on steady, sustainable changes like balanced vegan meals with plenty of vegetables, whole grains, legumes, and healthy fats, along with regular physical activity, rather than rapid weight loss.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep a night. Try to keep a consistent sleep and wake time, limit screens for an hour before bed, keep your bedroom cool and dark, and avoid caffeine in the afternoon or evening.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for 5-10 minutes a day, especially during stressful moments.
Try mindfulness or meditation apps, or simple grounding exercises, a few times a week.
Make time for activities you enjoy, like time in nature, hobbies, or connecting with friends and family.
behaviour_change: Keep a simple log of your meals, activity, and sleep to notice patterns and celebrate small wins.
Set one small, specific goal at a time, like adding a 10-minute walk after dinner, rather than trying to change everything at once.
Consider connecting with a dietitian familiar with vegan diets and East Asian food traditions to help personalize your meal planning.
Build a support network, whether friends, family, or a community group, to help you stay motivated over time.

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

preventive_actions: Aim for consistent physical activity most days of the week to help support healthy blood sugar levels
Follow your calorie target of about 1700 calories a day as a guide for balanced vegan meals
Schedule your vitamin B12 and cardiovascular risk assessment soon, since these are highlighted as priorities
Keep regular track of fasting and post-meal blood sugar readings to understand your patterns
Monitor your blood pressure and lipid profile regularly, since these connect closely to heart health
Work toward gradual, sustainable weight management as part of your overall plan

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
